tier_reason: The README's Benchmarks section lists only absolute Botan 'speed --msec=3000' throughputs (SHA-256 445.747 MiB/sec at 3.64 cycles/byte with GCC 7.3.1 on a Celeron J3455, 599.463 MiB/sec on the Kirin 620, 250.424 MiB/sec on POWER8) with no portable-C, OpenSSL or software-Botan row, so there is no measured speedup over any baseline; D.

corrections.caveats: No baseline measured: the README gives no portable-C, OpenSSL or software-only Botan row, and the numbers come from Botan ('concrete numbers are available from Jack Lloyd's Botan'); the README does not say which code path Botan was built with, so the link between these numbers and this repo's files is implied, not stated. The README itself says 'The speedups can be tricky to measure' and calls the Power8 numbers 'not that impressive'. No LICENSE file (raw LICENSE returns 404, GitHub shows no license); each source file header says 'Written and placed in public domain by Jeffrey Walton' (sha256-x86.c: 'Written and place in public domain'), with no patent grant. The x86 files are 'based on code from Intel, and by Sean Gulley for the miTLS project' and the ARM files on ARM and mbedTLS code, so the public-domain dedication of derived code is unverified. Maintenance: the 2026-01-08 commit reverts the 2026-01-07 merge of PR #14 (mikowals, opened 2024-02-24, a rename of ARM SHA-256 state variables that changes no calculation), so master's code is unchanged in substance since at least April 2018 (the commits before PR #14 are April 2018 .travis.yml tweaks); PR #16 with the same rename is still open. The x86 source header's own build line uses -msse4.1 -msha while the README says -msse4 -msha. Clang 3.7 ARM results are 'To be determined'.
corrections.hardware: Intel Celeron J3455 1.5 GHz (burst 2.2 GHz), ASUS J3455M-E; Kirin 620 SoC, octa-core Cortex-A53 1.2 GHz (the README names the ARM machine an ARMv8 LeMaker HiKey, the board that carries this SoC); ppc64le POWER8 at 3.4 GHz (GCC112, GCC compile farm)

notes: Numbers in claimed_speedup match the README exactly, but there is no baseline row anywhere, so the entry stays at D (keep with shortcoming 'no baseline measured'; the sha256.c reference implementation is never timed). The 2024 'ARM: fix incorrect variable names' change was merged 2026-01-07 and reverted 2026-01-08, so the code is effectively unchanged since 2018 even though the last-commit date reads active; 232 stars, 47 forks, not archived, not a fork.

tier_reason: Both BoringSSL commits time fiat-crypto field code against BoringSSL's previous curve25519 code with the public 'bssl speed -filter 25519' tool; 884086e is an independent measurement by BoringSSL's maintainer and b2c312d states clang, CMake Release and a 32-bit toolchain, but neither names a CPU model (b2c312d says 'Google Cloud's unidentified Intel Xeon with AVX2', 884086e names no hardware or compiler), so B and not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: No field-level speedup: parity or slightly slower. BoringSSL commit 884086e ('Remove x86_64 x25519 assembly', dated 2018-02-01): x86_64 assembly 15095.3 ops/sec base-point and 15094.0 ops/sec arbitrary-point multiplication versus fiat64 38817.1 and 13905.1 ops/sec; the message says 'The assembly is still about 9% faster than fiat64' and that fiat64 'gets to use the Ed25519 tables for the base point multiplication, so overall it is actually faster to disable the assembly' '(At the cost of touching a 30kB table.)'. The base-point win (about 2.6x, derived from page data) comes from that table-based algorithm, not from faster field arithmetic; one base-point plus one arbitrary-point multiplication works out to about 7547 ops/sec for the assembly versus about 10237 ops/sec for fiat64 (derived from page data; the commit gives no combined figure). Commit b2c312d ('curve25519: fiat-crypto field arithmetic.', dated 2017-11-03, 32-bit build): this branch 3546.5 / 3530.2 / 3014.5 ops/sec arbitrary-point and 11061.4 / 11226.2 / 8599.2 base-point versus master 3549.0 / 3551.9 / 3562.5 and 11177.1 / 11152.2 / 11306.7, i.e. parity; Ed25519 verify 2921.1 / 2919.0 / 2853.6 versus master 3055.7 / 3003.5 / 3058.6 ops/sec, about 4% slower (derived from page data); Ed25519 signing at parity (10759.3 / 10855.4 / 10807.0 versus 10840.8 / 10762.5 / 10863.2).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Commit b2c312d: CC=clang CXX=clang++ cmake -GNinja -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=../util/32-bit-toolchain.cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, then ninja and ./tool/bssl speed -filter 25519 (a 32-bit x86 build; compiler version not stated). Commit 884086e states no toolchain or flags.
corrections.hardware: Commit b2c312d: 'Google Cloud's unidentified Intel Xeon with AVX2' (two of the master runs are pasted from a shell prompt 'andreser@linux-andreser', so it is not certain every run shared one machine); commit 884086e states no CPU.
corrections.caveats: Evidence supports 'as fast as hand-written C, correct by construction', not 'faster': in 884086e the hand-written x86_64 assembly is still about 9% faster on arbitrary-point multiplication, and fiat64 wins base-point multiplication only by switching to the Ed25519 precomputed tables (a 30kB table), an algorithmic change rather than faster field code; in b2c312d the 32-bit fiat field code is at parity with master's C code (Ed25519 verify about 4% slower, derived from page data). Neither commit names a CPU model (tier B, not A); b2c312d was built with BoringSSL's 32-bit toolchain file, so it says nothing about 64-bit fiat code, and two of its master runs carry a shell prompt from the machine 'linux-andreser' (Andres Erbsen, fiat-crypto's lead author), so part of that data may be first-party and possibly from a different machine. Both measurements date from 2017-2018. The IEEE S&P 2019 paper (Erbsen et al.) and Jason Gross' thesis were not reachable (dspace.mit.edu, wireguard.com, ieee-security.org, adam.chlipala.net, moderncrypto.org, lists.zx2c4.com blocked here). Search snippets (snippet only) of Jason Donenfeld's 2018 kbench9000 runs report fiat64 at about 108,984 cycles per Curve25519 call against hacl64 about 109,782 and donna64 about 121,790 on a Skylake laptop, and in a later run on a Xeon E3-1505M v5 fiat64 about 144,106 against donna64 about 160,942 and hacl64 about 140,902, with the precomp_adx/precomp_bmi2 assembly fastest at roughly 117,000-121,000; fiat32 was roughly twice as slow as the 64-bit versions. Linux kernel commit 0ed42a6f431e ('crypto: curve25519 - generic C library implementations') takes the 32-bit Fiat and 64-bit HACL* code as 'the fastest available C implementations' without numbers. The repo README, boringssl_notes.md and folkwisdom.md contain no benchmark tables. Not OpenSSL itself: the baseline is BoringSSL's earlier curve25519 code. The repo now also ships fiat-amd64 (generated assembly), which was not evaluated here.

notes: Commit numbers match, but the record's 'commit's own combined figure 7547 to 10237 ops/sec' is not in the commit; it is a harmonic combination of the two rows and is now labelled derived. Keep with shortcoming 'not faster than the hand-written baseline (parity in C, about 9% slower than x86_64 asm on arbitrary-point; base-point win from a table algorithm)'; b2c312d was a 32-bit build and partly run on the fiat-crypto lead author's machine. Lead: Donenfeld's kbench9000 (git.zx2c4.com, not on GitHub) shows fiat64 about 1.12x faster than curve25519-donna64 (derived, snippet only); the S&P 2019 paper could lift this entry if a reachable copy turns up.
